mainTopic: Which stolen things carry כפל: birds, the word כל as a ריבוי, and what the listed details exclude
overview: The גמרא asks whether a thief who steals birds must pay כפל. It first tries to leave birds out, because each animal in the פסוק seems to be read on its own. It then shows that שור and חמור together would already cover all animals, so the extra word שה must come to include birds. The word כל in ״על כל דבר פשע״ is a ריבוי, so even non-kosher birds are included. The גמרא challenges this from the מעשר שני פסוק, where a ברייתא reads כל as part of a כלל ופרט וכלל. It gives two answers. First, בכל is a כלל while plain כל is a ריבוי. Second, the כל of כפל is special, because the section already has its own כלל ופרט וכלל, so the extra phrase must be a ריבוי. Finally, the גמרא explains the listed details: they exclude land, slaves, documents and items that are not clearly defined. ״על כל אבדה״ teaches רבי יוחנן's rule about someone who falsely claims a thief stole a lost item, and that rule continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Each animal in the verse is read separately, so birds are left out
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the argument that birds are not included in כפל, because each listed animal is treated as its own separate כלל ופרט.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because we read each and every one of them as its own generalization-and-detail. But birds are not included!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing out a line of reasoning from just before this, which argues that birds should not get כפל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists several animals: שור, חמור, שה. The claim is that each one is read as its own separate כלל ופרט, and each one only teaches 'things like this animal.' Since all the examples are animals, the expansion reaches other animals and stops there, so birds are left out.

keyTerms.meaning: A generalization and a specific detail, a method of reading a פסוק
We expound, we read in (a method of learning from a פסוק)

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not the גמרא's final view. It is the end of an argument that the גמרא is about to reject.

phrases.english: For each and every one
phrases.notes: He means each animal the פסוק lists: שור, חמור, שה (שמות 22:8).

phrases.english: as a generalization and detail by itself
we expound it;
but birds – no!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּהָא כֹּל חַד וְחַד כְּלָל וּפְרָט בְּאַפֵּי נַפְשֵׁיהּ דָּרְשִׁינַן לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an argument begun before this text that birds are excluded from כפל.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that birds are subject to כפל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If each listed animal is read as a separate כלל ופרט, the expansion only reaches animals, never birds.

steps.title: Then the Torah should have written only one example
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the reasoning: if the Torah only wanted animals, one animal would have been enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the Torah write just one detail!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the argument that birds are excluded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the goal were only to include animals, one listed animal would already teach that. The fact that the Torah lists several suggests it wants to include more than animals, meaning birds too.

phrases.english: If so,
let the Merciful One write one detail!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, נִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא חַד פְּרָטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 1's claim that birds are excluded.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The conclusion that birds are not subject to כפל.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Several examples would be extra wording if the Torah only meant animals; one would have been enough.

steps.title: No single animal would have been enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which one animal the Torah could have written, and shows that each one alone would teach too narrow a rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which one should the Torah have written? If it had written only 'ox,' I would think: an animal offered on the altar, yes; one not offered on the altar, no. And if it had written only 'donkey,' I would think: an animal whose firstborn is holy, yes; one whose firstborn is not holy, no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the idea that more than one animal was needed, so listing several animals does not prove that birds are included.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each animal has its own special feature. A שור can go on the מזבח, so writing only שור would limit כפל to altar animals. A חמור has קדושת בכורה (פטר חמור), so writing only חמור would limit כפל to animals with בכורה. So several examples were needed just to cover animals, and the argument in step 2 falls.

keyTerms.meaning: Brought as a sacrifice on the altar
Holy with the holiness of a firstborn

phrases.english: Which one should the Merciful One write?
If the Merciful One had written 'ox,'

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: קָרֵב לְגַבֵּי מִזְבֵּחַ – אִין,
phrases.english: I would have said: one offered on the altar – yes,
one not offered on the altar – no.
And if the Merciful One had written 'donkey,'
I would have said: one holy with firstborn status – yes,
phrases.notes: A firstborn donkey has special holiness (שמות 13:13), even though a donkey can't go on the altar.

phrases.english: one not holy with firstborn status – no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 2 by showing that one example would have been too limited.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 2's claim that one פרט would have been enough.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every single animal has a special feature that would wrongly narrow the rule, so more than one example was needed even to cover just animals.

steps.title: The extra word 'sheep' comes to include birds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: שור and חמור together would already cover all animals, so the extra word שה must be there to include birds.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: If so, let the Torah write 'ox and donkey.' Why do I need 'sheep'? Learn from this that it comes to include birds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 3 and reaches its conclusion: birds are subject to כפל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 showed that two examples were needed. But שור and חמור together would already solve that problem, since together they cover animals of both kinds. שה adds nothing about animals, so it must be teaching something new: that even birds get כפל.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from this, conclude from it

steps.whatToRemember: Only two examples (שור and חמור) were needed to cover all animals. The third example, שה, is extra, so it widens כפל to include birds.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source that a thief who steals birds must also pay כפל.

phrases.english: They say: If so,
let the Merciful One write 'ox and donkey,'
why do I need 'sheep'?
Conclude from it: to include birds.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: אִם כֵּן, נִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא ״שׁוֹר וַחֲמוֹר״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 3 and brings back step 2's point in a sharper form.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra wording in the פסוק (a word with nothing to teach about animals)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Several examples were needed just to cover animals, so birds are excluded.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two examples would cover animals. The third, שה, is extra and includes birds.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Birds are subject to כפל, learned from the extra word שה.

steps.title: Maybe only kosher birds are included
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that שה includes only kosher birds, which resemble a sheep in carrying טומאה, and not non-kosher birds.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say that שה comes to include only kosher birds, which are like a sheep, because a kosher bird's carcass makes clothes impure while it is being swallowed. Non-kosher birds have no such טומאה and do not make clothes impure while being swallowed, so they would not be included.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that the extra word שה includes birds, but asks why it should include all birds. Maybe it includes only kosher birds, which are more like a sheep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A source that includes things by comparison usually includes only what resembles the example. A sheep's carcass carries טומאה, and so does a kosher bird's נבלה, which makes a person's clothes impure while he swallows it. Non-kosher birds lack this טומאה, so the comparison would leave them out of כפל.

keyTerms.meaning: The throat, the place of swallowing

phrases.english: But say it comes to include kosher birds
which are similar to a sheep,
since it makes garments impure in the throat;
phrases.notes: A kosher bird's carcass makes the person eating it, and his clothes, impure while it goes down his throat.

phrases.english: but non-kosher birds
which have no impurity,
since they do not make garments impure in the throat,
no, they are not included!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that שה includes birds, then tries to narrow which birds.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that שה includes all birds in כפל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Something included by comparison should only include what resembles the example, so only kosher birds, which carry טומאה like a sheep, should be included.

steps.title: The word כל includes all birds
steps.stepSummary: The word כל in the פסוק is a ריבוי, so even non-kosher birds are included.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word כל is an inclusion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word כל in the פסוק of כפל widens the rule, so all birds are included, even non-kosher ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Comparison alone would have limited the rule to kosher birds. The word כל adds a ריבוי that removes this limit and brings in non-kosher birds as well.

keyTerms.meaning: An inclusion, a word that widens the law

phrases.english: "Any" is an inclusion.
phrases.notes: This is the word כל in "על כל דבר פשע", שמות 22:8.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the attempt to limit the inclusion to kosher birds.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only kosher birds, which resemble a sheep, are included.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word כל includes all birds, even non-kosher ones.

steps.title: Is כל always an inclusion?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that כל is always a ריבוי, because by מעשר the word כל is read as part of a כלל ופרט.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it true that wherever the Torah writes כל, it is an inclusion? But by מעשר, where כל is written, we read it as a כלל ופרט!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer. It points to the פסוק about מעשר money, where the word כל is treated as a כלל, a general statement, and not as a ריבוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כלל ופרט limits the law to things like the details. A ריבוי widens the law. If כל in the מעשר פסוק is a כלל, then כל does not automatically widen the law, so why treat it as a ריבוי here?

keyTerms.meaning: A general statement followed by specific details

phrases.english: And wherever it writes "any," is it an inclusion?
But regarding tithe, where "any" is written,
we expound it as a generalization and a detail!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer that כל is a ריבוי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that the word כל is a ריבוי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By מעשר, the word כל is read as a כלל in a כלל ופרט, so כל cannot automatically be a ריבוי.

steps.title: The ברייתא about spending מעשר money
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the מעשר שני פסוק as כלל ופרט וכלל and limits the purchases to things that grow from something that grew and get their food from the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: "And you shall give the money for whatever your soul desires" is a כלל. "For cattle, sheep, wine, and strong drink" is a פרט. "And for whatever your soul asks of you" is a second כלל. In a כלל ופרט וכלל, you include only what is like the פרט. Just as the items in the פרט grow from something that grew and get their food from the ground, so too anything that grows from something that grew and gets its food from the ground may be bought.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא that backs up its challenge. It shows that the word בכל in the מעשר פסוק is treated as a כלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא reads the פסוק as כלל ופרט וכלל, and that pattern includes only things similar to the details. Here the word כל plays the role of a כלל that is limited by the details, not a ריבוי that widens the law. This proves the point of the challenge in Step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: General, specific, general: include only what resembles the specific items
Produce from produce, something that grows from something that grew
Things that get their food from the ground

phrases.english: As it was taught: "And you shall give the money
phrases.notes: דברים 14:26, about spending מעשר שני money in ירושלים.

phrases.english: for whatever your soul desires" is a generalization,
"for cattle, for sheep, for wine, and for strong drink" is a detail,
"and for whatever your soul asks of you" generalizes again;
a generalization, a detail, and a generalization:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט,
phrases.english: you include only what is similar to the detail,
just as the detail is clearly defined as
produce from produce and grown from the ground,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל פְּרִי מִפְּרִי וְגִידּוּלֵי קַרְקַע.
phrases.english: so too anything that is produce from produce and grown from the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the challenge in Step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That כל can be read as a כלל rather than a ריבוי
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on מעשר שני, דברים 14:26

steps.title: בכל is a כלל, but כל is a ריבוי
steps.stepSummary: First answer: the form בכל is a כלל, while plain כל is a ריבוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: בכל is a כלל, but כל is an inclusion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by pointing to a small difference in the wording. The מעשר פסוק says בכל, which is a כלל, while the כפל פסוק says plain כל, which is a ריבוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed both פסוקים use the same word. This answer says the extra letter ב changes how the word is read, so the מעשר ברייתא does not disprove the ריבוי by כפל.

phrases.english: They say: "for whatever" is a generalization,
"any" is an inclusion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from מעשר by telling apart the two forms of the word.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: כל and בכל are the same, so the מעשר ברייתא proves כל is a כלל.
steps.terutzMaskana: בכל is a כלל, but כל is a ריבוי.

steps.title: Usually a כלל, but here a ריבוי
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: כל is normally a כלל, but the כל in the פסוק of כפל is a ריבוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: כל is a כלל, but the כל here is an inclusion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer. It agrees that כל is normally a כלל, but says that the כל in the פסוק of כפל is an exception and works as a ריבוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not rely on the letter ב. It accepts the general rule that כל is a כלל and limits the ריבוי to this specific פסוק. Steps 11 and 12 explain why this כל is different.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say, introducing a second answer

steps.whatToRemember: Both answers keep the conclusion that the word כל in the פסוק of כפל includes even non-kosher birds. They differ only on whether כל is usually a ריבוי or usually a כלל.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: "any" is a generalization,
but the "any" here is an inclusion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the challenge from מעשר, different from Step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since כל is usually a כלל, it cannot be a ריבוי by כפל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if כל is usually a כלל, the כל in the כפל פסוק is a ריבוי.

steps.title: Setting up the proof: an earlier כלל ופרט וכלל already exists
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the guarding section already opens with its own כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: After all, a כלל ופרט וכלל is already written at the beginning. ״If a man gives his neighbor″ is a כלל. ״Money or vessels″ is a פרט. ״To guard″ goes back and makes another כלל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a proof for its answer that the כל in the פסוק of כפל is a ריבוי. First it shows that the opening פסוק of the section is already built as a כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״כי יתן איש אל רעהו″ is broad, ״כסף או כלים″ narrows it, and ״לשמור″ widens it again. This matters because if the Torah wanted a כלל ופרט, it already had one here. The next step uses this fact.

keyTerms.meaning: After all, consider this (opens a line of reasoning)
A general term, a specific detail, and another general term: a rule for reading פסוקים

phrases.english: After all, it is written at the beginning
a general term, a detail, and a general term,

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״כִּי יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ״ – כָּלַל,
phrases.english: as it is written: "If a man gives his neighbor" — a general term,
"money or vessels" — a detail,
"to guard" — it went back and made a general term again;
phrases.notes: הדר and חזר both mean "went back." Some versions say the word in round brackets; the corrected wording uses the one in square brackets.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּדֵי כְּתִיב מֵעִיקָּרָא כְּלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the proof for Step 10's claim that the כל of כפל is a ריבוי
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the כל in ״על כל דבר פשע״ is a ריבוי
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 22:6, which is already structured as a כלל ופרט וכלל

steps.title: The extra phrase must be a ריבוי
steps.stepSummary: If ״על כל דבר פשע״ were only a כלל ופרט, its details could have been added to the earlier one, so it must be a ריבוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think ״על כל דבר פשע״ also comes as a כלל ופרט, the Torah should have written these details together with that earlier כלל ופרט. Why do I need ״על כל דבר פשע״? Learn from this that it is a ריבוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its proof. Because the Torah wrote a separate phrase with כל, that כל must be a ריבוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah does not waste words. If the only goal were a כלל ופרט, the details (ox, donkey, sheep, garment) could have been placed in the existing כלל ופרט וכלל of the earlier פסוק. A new phrase starting with כל shows it has a different job: to include more, like a ריבוי.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
An inclusion, a word that adds more cases

steps.whatToRemember: The כל in the פסוק of כפל is a ריבוי because a plain כלל ופרט would have been redundant with the earlier פסוק.
steps.whyThisMatters: This backs up Step 10's answer and explains why the case of כפל is read differently from מעשר.

phrases.english: And if it enters your mind
that this "for any matter of trespass"
also comes for a general term and a detail,
let the Merciful One write these details
phrases.notes: These are ox, donkey, sheep and garment, listed in that same פסוק.

phrases.english: together with that general term and detail;
why do I need "for any matter of trespass"?
Learn from it: it is an inclusion.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ הַאי ״עַל כׇּל דְּבַר פֶּשַׁע״ נָמֵי לִכְלָל וּפְרָט הוּא דַּאֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof that Step 11 set up
steps.raayaObject: That the כל in the פסוק of כפל is a ריבוי
steps.raayaSupportSource: The redundancy argument: a second כלל ופרט would be unnecessary

steps.title: If כל includes everything, why list the details?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק lists ox, donkey, sheep and garment if כל already includes everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you said כל is a ריבוי, why do I need all these details?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges its own conclusion. If כל includes everything, the list of details seems useless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a ריבוי reading, the broad word does the work of including. That leaves the specific items (ox, donkey, sheep, garment) without an obvious job, and the Torah does not write words for nothing.

phrases.english: Now that you said "any" is an inclusion,
why do I need all these details?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא דְּאָמְרַתְּ ״כֹּל״ – רִיבּוּיָא, כֹּל הָנֵי פְּרָטֵי לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges a consequence of Step 12's conclusion
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of כל as a ריבוי in the פסוק of כפל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If כל includes everything, the specific details in the פסוק appear to have no purpose

steps.title: Each detail comes to exclude something
steps.stepSummary: The three animals exclude land, slaves and documents, and the garment excludes an item that is not clearly defined.
steps.simpleTranslation: One animal excludes land, one excludes slaves, and one excludes documents. ״Garment″ excludes an item that is not clearly defined.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Each detail in the פסוק has a job: it limits the ריבוי by leaving something out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even with כל as a ריבוי, the details narrow it. Each of the three animals (ox, donkey, sheep) rules out one category: קרקע, עבדים and שטרות. The garment, which has a clear size and shape, rules out a דבר שאינו מסוים, an item that cannot be clearly identified or measured.

keyTerms.meaning: An item that is not clearly defined in size or amount

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the details stop the ריבוי from working. כל still includes a lot; the details only cut out these specific categories.

phrases.english: One is to exclude land,
and one is to exclude slaves,
and one is to exclude documents.
"Garment" is to exclude an item that is not clearly defined,

steps.triggerLanguage: חַד לְמַעוֹטֵי קַרְקַע, וְחַד לְמַעוֹטֵי עֲבָדִים, וְחַד לְמַעוֹטֵי שְׁטָרוֹת
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns each detail a limiting job within the ריבוי
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The details are pointless once כל is a ריבוי
steps.terutzMaskana: Each detail excludes a category: land, slaves, documents, and undefined items

steps.title: ״על כל אבדה″ teaches the rule of רבי חייא בר אבא
steps.stepSummary: The phrase ״על כל אבדה″ is needed for a teaching of רבי חייא בר אבא in the name of רבי יוחנן about someone who claims a thief stole the item.
steps.simpleTranslation: ״For any lost item″ is for the teaching of רבי חייא בר אבא. רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: one who makes the claim that a thief stole...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues its answer by explaining the last phrase in the פסוק, ״על כל אבדה″. It begins quoting רבי יוחנן's rule about a טוען טענת גנב, and the quote continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This phrase is not a limiting detail like the others. It is used for a separate law. Since the phrase speaks of a lost item (אבדה), the law concerns someone holding a lost item who falsely claims that a thief took it. The rest of רבי יוחנן's rule continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: For the teaching of רבי so-and-so
One who claims that a thief stole the item
